entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 20

 2Ch 20:1-21 . Jehoshaphat, Invaded by the Moabites, Proclaims a Fast.

 1. the children of Moab ... Ammon, and with them other beside the Ammonites-- supposed to be rather the name of a certain people called Mohammonim or Mehunim ( 2Ch 26:7 ), who dwelt in Mount Seir--either a branch of the old Edomite race or a separate tribe who were settled there.
entries.reader_content_plain:
CHAPTER 20

 2Ch 20:1-21 . Jehoshaphat, Invaded by the Moabites, Proclaims a Fast.

 1. the children of Moab ... Ammon, and with them other beside the Ammonites-- supposed to be rather the name of a certain people called Mohammonim or Mehunim ( 2Ch 26:7 ), who dwelt in Mount Seir--either a branch of the old Edomite race or a separate tribe who were settled there.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4045"/><div sID="gen5860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4045"/><hi type="bold">2. from beyond the sea on this side Syria--</hi>Instead of "Syria," some versions read "Edom," and many able critics prefer this reading, both because the nomad tribes here mentioned were far from Syria, and because express mention is made of Mount Seir, that is, Edom. The meaning then is: this confederate horde was composed of the different tribes that inhabited the far distant regions bordering on the northern and eastern coasts of the Red Sea. Their progress was apparently by the southern point of the Dead Sea, as far as En-gedi, which, more anciently, was called Hazezon-tamar (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.7">Ge 14:7</reference>). This is the uniform route taken by the Arabs in their marauding expeditions at the present day; and in coming round the southern end of the Dead Sea, they can penetrate along the low-lying Ghor far north, without letting their movements be known to the tribes and villages west of the mountain chain [Robinson]. Thus, anciently, the invading horde in Jehoshaphat's time had marched as far north as En-gedi, before intelligence of their advance was conveyed to the court. En-gedi is recognized in the modern Ainjidy and is situated at a point of the western shore, nearly equidistant from both extremities of the lake [Robinson]. <div eID="gen5860" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4046"/><div sID="gen5861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4046"/><hi type="bold">3-4. Jehoshaphat ... proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah--</hi>Alarmed by the intelligence and conscious of his total inability to repel this host of invaders, Jehoshaphat felt his only refuge was at the horns of the altar. He resolved to employ the aid of his God, and, in conformity with this resolution, he summoned all his subjects to observe a solemn fast at the sanctuary. It was customary with the Hebrew kings to proclaim fasts in perilous circumstances, either in a city, a district, or throughout the entire kingdom, according to the greatness of the emergency. On this occasion, it was a universal fast, which extended to infants (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.13">2Ch 20:13</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="Joel.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.7">Jon 3:7</reference>). <div eID="gen5861" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4055"/><div sID="gen5871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4055"/><hi type="bold">22. when they began to sing and to praise the Lord set ambushments against the children of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir--</hi>Some think that this was done by angels in human form, whose sudden appearance diffused an uncontrollable panic. Others entertain the more probable opinion that, in the camp of this vast horde, composed of different tribes, jealousies and animosities had sprung up, which led to widespread dissensions and fierce feuds, in which they drew the sword against each other. The consequence was, that as the mutual strife commenced when the Hebrew procession set out from Jerusalem, the work of destruction was completed before Jehoshaphat and his people arrived at the battlefield. Thus easy is it for God to make the wrath of man to praise Him, to confound the counsels of His enemies and employ their own passions in defeating the machinations they have devised for the overthrow of His Church and people. <div eID="gen5871" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4060"/><div sID="gen5877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4060"/><hi type="bold">35-37. after this did Jehoshaphat ... join himself with Ahaziah ... to make ships--</hi>A combined fleet was built at Ezion-geber, the destination of which was to voyage to Tartessus, but it was wrecked. Jehoshaphat's motive for entering into this partnership was to secure a free passage through Israel, for the vessels were to be conveyed across the Isthmus of Suez, and to sail to the west of Europe from one of the ports of Palestine on the Mediterranean. Eliezer, a prophet, denounced this unholy alliance, and foretold, as divine judgment, the total wreck of the whole fleet. The consequence was, that although Jehoshaphat broke off--in obedience to the divine will--his league with Ahaziah, he formed a new scheme of a merchant fleet, and Ahaziah wished to be admitted a partner [1Ki 22:48]. The proposal of the Israelitish king was respectfully declined [1Ki 22:49]. The destination of this new fleet was to Ophir, because the Israelitish seaports were not accessible to him for the Tartessus trade; but the ships, when just off the docks, were wrecked in the rocky creek of Ezion-geber. <chapter eID="2Chr.20"/>
